config.title: Merge Sorted Arrays

intro.title: Merge Sorted Arrays
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that merges two already-sorted arrays into a single sorted array. You will learn the core concept of the two-pointer technique, a common algorithmic pattern for efficiently processing sorted data. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, while loops, and conditional logic. This beginner-friendly exercise will help you practice comparing elements and building a result step-by-step.
intro.usecase: The merge sorted arrays algorithm is essential in data processing scenarios where you need to combine multiple sorted datasets into a single sorted result. This pattern appears in e-commerce platforms when merging product search results from different categories or filters into a unified, sorted display. It's also used in social media feeds that combine posts from multiple sources (friends, groups, followed pages) into a single chronological timeline. Database systems frequently employ this technique when merging results from sorted indexes during query execution.

objectives: Implement a function that merges two sorted arrays into a single sorted array
Apply two-pointer technique to traverse both arrays simultaneously
Construct conditional logic to compare elements from both arrays
Initialize and manipulate result arrays while maintaining sorted order
Integrate edge case handling for arrays of different lengths
Control loop execution until all elements from both arrays are processed
Configure the merge algorithm to handle empty array inputs

content.body: Imagine you're looking for a specific word in a dictionary. You wouldn't start at page 1 and read every word. Instead, you'd open to the middle and eliminate half the book each time. That's binary search! Today we'll learn this powerful algorithm for finding items in sorted arrays.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain why binary search requires sorted data
• Implement binary search to find a target value
• Handle cases when the target isn't found
• Visualize how the search space halves each step
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's play a guessing game. I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100. Your goal is to find it with the fewest guesses possible. What's your first guess?
content.title: Try it yourself

content.body: If I tell you my number is 73, and you guessed 50, what should you do next? Should you check numbers 1-49 or 51-100? Why?
content.title: Think strategically

content.body: Now I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 1000. If your first guess is 500 and I say 'too low,' what range remains? How many numbers did you eliminate with one guess?
content.title: One more round

content.body: You instinctively used a 'divide and conquer' approach. Instead of checking every number from 1 to 100, you started in the middle and eliminated half the possibilities with each guess.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Checking every element works for small arrays, but what if you have 10 million sorted items? Linear search would take forever. Binary search finds any item in just ~24 comparisons!
content.title: Why it matters

content.body: Binary search works because the data is sorted. When we check the middle element, we can instantly know whether our target must be in the left half or right half. We repeatedly cut the search range in half until we find what we're looking for or determine it's not there.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Repeatedly cut the range in half; only one half can contain the answer.

content.body: Here's how binary search works: Start with the entire array. Calculate the middle index. Compare the middle element to your target. If it matches, you're done! If the target is smaller, search the left half. If larger, search the right half. Repeat until found or the range is empty.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Set left = 0, right = array.length - 1
2. While left <= right:
   a. Calculate mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2)
   b. If array[mid] equals target, return mid
   c. If target < array[mid], set right = mid - 1
   d. If target > array[mid], set left = mid + 1
3. If loop ends, return -1 (not found)
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the search boundaries
steps.instruction: Initialize the left and right pointers that will track our search range. Left starts at the first index (0), right at the last index.
steps.hint: Remember: array indices start at 0, so the last index is length - 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should have left and right variables defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Remember to define both left and right variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need two variables: left starting at 0, right starting at arr.length - 1.

steps.title: Create the search loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as there's still a range to search. The loop runs while left <= right.
steps.hint: We use <= because when left equals right, there's still one element to check.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should have a while loop with the correct condition.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Check your loop condition - it should run while left <= right.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need to keep searching as long as left is less than or equal to right.

steps.title: Calculate the midpoint
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, calculate the middle index. Use Math.floor() to ensure we get an integer index.
steps.hint: The formula is: mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2)
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should calculate mid inside the loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure to use Math.floor() and the correct formula.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. We need: let mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2);

steps.title: Compare and adjust range
steps.instruction: Add the comparison logic. If we find the target, return its index. Otherwise, adjust left or right to eliminate half the search space.
steps.hint: Three cases: found (return mid), target smaller (right = mid - 1), target larger (left = mid + 1).
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should have the comparison logic with three branches.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Remember all three cases: equal, less than, and greater than.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's break it down: if arr[mid] === target, return mid. If target < arr[mid], right = mid - 1. Otherwise, left = mid + 1.

steps.title: Handle not found case
steps.instruction: After the loop ends (meaning we didn't find the target), return -1 to indicate the target isn't in the array.
steps.hint: The return -1 goes after the while loop, not inside it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should return -1 after the loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. We need to return -1 to indicate the target wasn't found.
steps.feedbackWrong: After the loop ends without finding the target, add: return -1;

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented binary search. Remember: it only works on sorted arrays, cuts the search space in half each step, and returns -1 when the target isn't found. With 1 million items, binary search needs only ~20 comparisons versus 1 million for linear search!
